qs.q: Which of these could NOT be the raw material for a spirit?
o: Sea salt
Potatoes
Rice
Dates, rich in natural sugars
qs.e: Potatoes and rice hold starch to convert, dates ready sugars: all could in principle become a spirit. Without carbohydrates, yeast would have nothing to turn into alcohol.

qs.q: What do the choices about what to keep and what to reject depend on?
o: The distiller's preferences and the type of spirit
Only on the yeast used in fermentation
A fixed rule that is the same for every spirit
The outside temperature
qs.e: There is no single rule: one distiller may want a wider, richer heart, another a cleaner, lighter one. Yeast affects which congeners exist but does not decide the cuts. Climate does not decide what to keep.

qs.q: What happens to the watery liquid left in the pot after the first distillation?
o: It is discarded
It is added to the low wines
It is used to dilute the heart
It is kept with the heads and tails for the next batch
qs.e: Only the heads and tails of the second distillation are recycled, as they still hold ethanol and useful aromas. The residue is almost pure water. Spirits are diluted with completely pure water.

qs.q: A distillery wants a characterful spirit but only has a column still. What should it do?
o: Draw the heart from a lower-strength plate
Draw the heart from the highest plate, as close to the top as possible
Add more plates to raise the strength
Give up: it cannot be done in a column
qs.e: The higher the draw-off, the higher the strength and the more neutral the spirit; adding plates pushes the same way. Armagnac, Bourbon and rhum agricole show that a column can give plenty of character.

qs.q: Which flavouring technique also extracts colour from botanicals?
o: Maceration
Redistillation
Redistillation in a vacuum still at low temperature
Activated charcoal filtration
qs.e: Colour is not volatile, so it does not pass through any distillation, even under vacuum. Activated charcoal, on the contrary, removes colour.

qs.q: Why are the congeners with a boiling point similar to ethanol so important?
o: They give the spirit its distinctive character
They give the spirit its colour
They smell of solvent and must be removed
They make the newly made spirit sweeter
qs.e: A newly made spirit is colourless and dry, so these congeners give neither colour nor sweetness. The solvent smell belongs to the more volatile heads.

qs.q: Each congener reaches a plate where it is the least volatile. What happens above that plate?
o: Its concentration falls away quickly
Its concentration keeps rising
It turns into ethanol
It stays the same on every plate up to the top
qs.e: This spreads congeners along the height: the most volatile at the top, the least volatile low down. So the higher the draw, the fewer aromas. Congeners do not turn into ethanol.

qs.q: A bartender wants a colourless Armagnac with lively fruit for a cocktail. What fits?
o: A Blanche, perhaps from Folle Blanche
A vintage Armagnac from a very old year
An XO Armagnac charcoal-filtered to strip out its colour
A Ténarèze Armagnac aged in new barrels
qs.e: Blanche is made like other Armagnacs but without oak ageing. An old vintage or an Armagnac aged in new barrels will have colour and woody notes. Filtering an XO to remove its colour would not make it a recognised style and would strip out much of its aroma.

qs.q: Which comparison between grappa and Calvados maturation is correct?
o: Grappa usually rests in inert vessels; Calvados matures in oak
Both mature in large oak vessels that give little oak
Grappa matures in oak, Calvados in steel
Both are bottled with no rest at all
qs.e: Large oak vessels are typical of Calvados, not grappa. The other two options reverse or erase what really happens. Even the simplest grappa rests at least briefly in inert vessels before bottling.

qs.q: An American label reads '90 proof'. What is the alcoholic strength?
o: 45% abv
90% abv
40% abv
50% abv
qs.e: Simply halve the proof figure. 90% abv would mean confusing the two scales, while 40% abv is 80 proof and 50% abv is 100 proof.

qs.q: Which group of descriptors usually signals a peated whisky?
o: Medicinal, smoked fish, seaweed
Vanilla, coconut, sweet spice
Pear, apple, white flowers
Rye bread, lemon zest, peppercorn and other spices
qs.e: Vanilla and coconut come from oak, especially ex-bourbon. Pear and apple are fruity, not peaty. Rye bread and lemon describe American rye whiskey.

qs.q: Under international laws and agreements, what can anyone expect on seeing the word 'whisky' on a label, in any country?
o: That it is made from grain
That it was aged at least three years in Scotland
That it contains at least 51% corn, as international rules require
That it was distilled in a pot still
qs.e: Three years in Scotland applies only to Scotch, 51% corn only to bourbon and Tennessee. Pot stills are required for Scottish single malt, but many whiskies worldwide use column stills.

qs.q: Why is molasses diluted with water before fermentation?
o: Its sugar content is too high to ferment
To remove its dark colour before distillation
To lower its acidity, which would kill all the yeast
To produce a low-strength rum straight away
qs.e: The water brings the sugar down to a level at which yeast can work. Colour is not removed at this stage, and the rum's strength depends on distillation, not on how the molasses is diluted. Acidity is not the reason for adding water.

qs.q: When is the ideal time to harvest agave?
o: At peak maturity, just before it flowers
Just after flowering, when the stalk is tallest
In its first year, when the leaves are most tender
Any time at all, since maturity makes no difference
qs.e: After flowering the inulin is used up and the plant dies. A young plant has not yet built reserves or aromas. The leaves are thrown away anyway.

qs.q: What kind of process is vodka distillation usually?
o: Continuous
Batch-based, in clay stills
A single pot still pass at low strength
Triple pot distillation, as required by law
qs.e: Some small distillers work in batches with a pot still before the column, but that is the exception. A single low-strength pass would give a characterful spirit, the opposite of vodka.

qs.q: What always appears prominently on a grappa label?
o: The word grappa
The harvest year
The type of oak used for the compulsory ageing
The term Hors d'âge
qs.e: The grape variety may appear next to it, but a vintage is not a typical element. There is no compulsory oak ageing: classic grappa never sees wood. Hors d'âge is a Cognac age term.

qs.q: Which of the five Scotch whisky regions is an island?
o: Islay
Speyside
Lowland
Campbeltown, on the mainland's west coast
qs.e: Speyside, Lowland and Campbeltown are on the mainland. Islay is also the only region whose name is a fairly reliable style clue, thanks to peat.

qs.q: Why did the French islands develop a tradition of cane juice rum?
o: France favoured sugar from beet
Local molasses was too poor and acidic to ferment
The French Navy demanded a much lighter rum
Modern columns arrived there before anywhere else
qs.e: France protected its own beet farmers, so the islands' cane juice was not needed by the sugar industry. The naval ration belongs to the British tradition, and modern columns are linked instead to the Cuban style.

qs.q: Which group lists the countries historically linked to vodka?
o: Russia, Poland, Finland, Sweden
Russia, France, Ireland, Mexico
Scotland, Japan, Canada, the USA
Poland, Brazil, Jamaica, Cuba
qs.e: They still make large volumes and many of the most highly regarded vodkas, although excellent examples are now found almost everywhere. The other groups mix in countries famous for whisky, Cognac, agave spirits or rum.

qs.q: What colour is the great majority of bottled gin?
o: Colourless
Pale lemon
Light amber
Faint green from the botanicals
qs.e: Pale lemon applies only to the small niche of oak-aged gins. Amber would require long ageing, which is not typical of gin. Botanicals give colour only through maceration, not through distillation.

qs.q: A liqueur is flavoured with apricot kernels. Which group does it belong to?
o: Seed, nut and kernel
Fruit, because the apricot is a fruit
Herb
Cream
qs.e: It is a trap: the apricot is a fruit, but the kernel has an almond-like flavour, unlike the flesh. The group depends on which part of the plant gives the flavour. Herb and cream do not apply.

qs.q: What has driven the recent wave of new, innovative aromatised wines?
o: The growing popularity of cocktails
A new European law banning wormwood
A shortage of neutral, high-acid white grapes
Almost all production moving away from the Alpine area
qs.e: Wormwood-family plants are in fact compulsory for vermouth in Europe. No grape shortage explains the trend. And the vast majority of these wines is still made in the Alpine area of France and Italy, even though they are now made everywhere.

qs.q: What is the bottle pourer on frequently used bottles for?
o: It limits the flow, making accurate pouring into a jigger easier
It filters out impurities
It chills the spirit as it pours
It replaces the jigger entirely
qs.e: It neither filters nor chills the liquid. It works together with the jigger, which remains the tool for consistent measuring. Without a measure, cocktails would lose consistency.

qs.q: What are the core ingredients of a Whisky Sour?
o: Bourbon or rye, lemon, simple syrup
Scotch, sweet vermouth, bitters
Whisky, sugar and bitters, stirred and served in a tumbler
Whisky, ginger ale, bitters
qs.e: Scotch, sweet vermouth and bitters make a Rob Roy; whisky, sugar and bitters an Old Fashioned; whisky and ginger ale with bitters a Horse's Neck. Only the Whisky Sour has the citrus juice typical of sours.

qs.q: Why does a spirit's appearance say little about its type, quality or age?
o: Colour can be altered afterwards
All spirits share the same amber colour
The glass always changes the shade
Colour only appears once water is added
qs.e: Spirits range from colourless to brown and beyond, so they do not share one colour. A good glass does not alter the shade. Appearance is in fact judged before adding water.
